extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers submitting fiction to The New Yorker
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for submitting literary short stories to The New Yorker, including stylistic, thematic, and format requirements. Targets finished, polished stories in the 2,000–10,000 word range with a distinctive literary voice and mastery of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary fiction (priority over plot-driven work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction — character development, nuanced themes, compelling prose over plot-driven narratives
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stories emphasizing character interiority, thematic nuance, and craft rather than genre-style plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polished, distinctive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Polished, distinctive voice — carefully controlled tone
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice should be singular and controlled; the narrative tone must feel intentional and consistent throughout the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original voices and perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Original voices and perspectives — avoid stories too similar to other published works
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors look for fresh perspectives and avoid stories that feel derivative or closely mirror previously published pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of language — flawless grammar, spelling, clarity, tense
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should demonstrate technical command of prose: correct mechanics, clear syntax, consistent tense, and precise diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polished finished drafts only
rubrics_metrics.description: Polished finished drafts — submit only your very best work
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit rough or early drafts. Only send work you consider professionally complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique storytelling
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should show originality in structure, perspective, or approach to material—something that distinguishes them from typical submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories that resonate beyond the page
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that resonate beyond the page
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stories that leave lasting impressions, provoke thought, or suggest significance beyond the immediate plot events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for literary realism and observed detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Often: literary realism, character interiority, observed detail of class/family/place
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many accepted stories emphasize realistic depiction, attention to social/sexual/class detail, and intimate psychological observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring thematic interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Often interlocking themes of identity, mortality, alienation, intimacy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not mandatory, themes around identity, mortality, alienation, and intimacy frequently recur in favored work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude genre fiction (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre fiction (sci-fi, fantasy, romance, thriller) — with rare exceptions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine generally does not publish conventional genre stories; exceptions are uncommon and must be literary in execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimental or clichéd MFA tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimental, MFA-cliché stories
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimental or formulaic 'MFA workshop' pieces are discouraged; strive for specificity and emotional honesty rather than familiar tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plot-twist-driven work without craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot-twist-driven work without literary craft
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that rely on gimmicky twists rather than sustained literary craft are unlikely to be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Word count: 2,000–10,000 words (most stories ~4,000–8,000)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit within the 2,000–10,000 word range; note that most accepted pieces fall between roughly 4,000 and 8,000 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise cover letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover letter: 1–3 sentences (name, brief credits, title, word count)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep cover letters short and factual: include your name, brief publication credits (if any), story title, and word count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Online portal only
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker accepts fiction submissions only via its online submission portal; follow the portal’s instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong opening sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong opening sentences that imply a whole world
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings should quickly suggest a wider world or situation, creating immediate interest and narrative promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression — economical storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Compression — no wasted scene or description
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every scene and detail should serve the story; editors favor tight, economical prose without filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resonant, often ambiguous endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Resonant, often ambiguous endings (not punchlines)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings should feel earned and resonant rather than gimmicky punchlines; ambiguity is often preferable to neat closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subtext
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtext — things implied rather than stated
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective stories suggest meaning indirectly; rely on implication and layered detail rather than explicit exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity of detail — particularized place and class
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, particular details about place, class, and social context help ground the story and create verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral or psychological stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: A felt sense of moral or psychological stakes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should convey meaningful stakes—ethical, emotional, or psychological—that make the narrative matter to readers.
